text:
These wolves in Alaska ate all the deer. Then, they did something unexpected (hunting sea otters) | Mihai Andrei, ZME Science

Pleasant Island in Alaska is not exactly befitting of its name. The frigid, 20-square-mile island is uninhabited by humans, but it hosts a remarkably large and rich ecosystem that features deer, otters, red squirrels, and even brown bears. But in 2013, the island got a new addition: wolves.

When wolves colonized the island in 2013, it set up a natural experiment.

“This provided a great opportunity to study predator-prey dynamics of wolves and deer,” says Gretchen Roffler, a wildlife research biologist with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game. “We were interested in seeing how the newly colonizing wolf population would impact the deer population and predicted that the wolves might eat all the deer, and then leave the island as it is only separated from the mainland by 1.5 km.”

The first part of the prediction came true. The deer population of around 120-200 deer plummeted. The island’s deer had already been hit hard by an exceptionally severe winter in 2006–2007, but researchers concluded that sustained wolf predation after 2013 was ultimately responsible for their disappearance.

But instead of moving to greener pastures, the wolves remained on an island and shifted their diet to unexpected prey: sea otters.

A marine predator becomes prey

Sea otters are themselves a top predator in the near-shore ecosystem, while wolves are an apex predator in the terrestrial area. — so it’s pretty surprising that you end up with a dynamic where one eats the other, says Taal Levi, an associate professor at Oregon State. “You have top predators feeding on a top predator,” Levi says.

Gretchen, Levi, and colleagues were studying wolf diets throughout southeast Alaska. The work also has an important conservation-management dimension. Alexander Archipelago wolves have been petitioned for federal protection several times, but in August 2023 the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service concluded that listing the subspecies under the Endangered Species Act was not warranted.

They tracked some of the wolves with GPS collars and analyzed their scat. They found that in 2015, deer were the primary food of wolves, representing 75% of their diet. By 2017, wolves transitioned to eating primarily sea otters (57% of their diet), while deer only made up 7% of their diet. The pattern held through to 2020, when the study ended.

Otters themselves have had a rough history in the area. During the 19th and 20th centuries, sea otters in the region were hunted by fur traders and basically wiped out from the region. Local wolves were not hunted to extinction, unlike wolves in other parts of the US. But it was only in recent decades, thanks to the legal protection granted to sea otters, that the two populations overlapped.

But researchers weren’t expecting wolves, a terrestrial species, to become so proficient at eating sea otters — which, as the name implies, spend most of their time at sea.

“They are both scavenging otters and hunting them when the sea otters haul on land. Sea otters are very unlikely to be vulnerable to wolves in the ocean,” notes Levi.

Wolves were often seen patrolling the shoreline of Pleasant Island and investigating rocky outcrops. The GPS data confirmed that they spent a lot of time in the intertidal zone as if looking for something — and indeed they were: they were looking for otters to ambush.

Sea otters haul out on rocks to conserve energy, says Roffler. But this makes them more vulnerable to predation as they are slow and awkward on land — and wolves are quick to take their chance. “We have collected evidence of wolves killing sea otters by ambush when they haul out on land or are in shallow water,” Gretchen adds.

This new twist to the ecosystem makes for a very interesting case study, Gretchen continues.

“Previously there have been investigations into the effects of marine predators on sea otter populations, but until now very little attention has been paid to the impact of terrestrial predators on sea otters, or how sea otters may be an abundant marine prey to terrestrial predators. This interaction was unexpected, but has had profound effects, at least on Pleasant Island.”

For now, it’s not clear how the otters are adapting to this (or if they are adapting at all). The biggest effect might be a behavioral change that forces them to spend more time at sea, even when it would be beneficial to them to conserve energy on land — the effects of this could be stressful in the long term, but this is something that warrants future research, Levi says.

But overall, the researchers don’t expect that wolves will have a big effect on the sea otter population. The more important ecosystem implication is that wolf population dynamics can be decoupled from the large mammals that make up their typical prey.

“This allows wolves to remain abundant even as they cause large herbivore populations to decline. That is, sea otters may allow wolves to maintain large herbivores at lower densities, which has implications for vegetation and the animals that depend on it (bees, birds, bears for floral and berry resources, for example), across a huge coastline that will be eventually occupied by sea otters as their recovery continues,” Levi adds.

This surprising finding of wolf diets definitely warrants more studies to better understand the interactions in this ecosystem — and Levi says they’re working exactly on that.

“We are now increasingly following up on the wolf-sea otter story with additional field studies, including one by PhD student Ellen Dymit, comparing mainland study areas with and without sea otters along the colonizing front of sea otter population expansion.”

Turns out, the behavior isn’t even limited to Pleasant Island. Researchers have now documented wolves eating sea otters at several sites along Alaska’s coast. Near Gustavus, a nine-wolf pack killed 31 sea otters during eight month-long study periods between 2019 and 2024 — including 26 in just one month in 2022 — even though moose were still available.

The same pattern showed up elsewhere: wolves ate more sea otters in places where otters were abundant, including Glacier Bay and coastal Katmai, and very few where otters were scarce, such as Lake Clark. That suggests sea otters may be becoming a regular food source for coastal wolves, rather than an unusual fallback on one island. These broader results are still preliminary and have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed study.

A toxic trade-off

But there may be a cost to relying so heavily on marine prey: contaminant exposure.. A 2025 study reports that switching to marine prey leads to unprecedented mercury concentrations. The otter-eating wolves on Pleasant Island pack had mercury concentrations nearly 8 times as high as reported in Arctic wolf hair.

Methylmercury is produced in aquatic ecosystems, primarily by microbes in sediments and water bodies. The aquatic food chain magnifies mercury concentrations, meaning predators at the top, like sea otters, accumulate high levels of it. When wolves consume marine mammals such as sea otters, they absorb the mercury that has built up along the food chain.

Pleasant Island wolves had an average total-mercury concentration of 17.59 ppm in their livers. That was seven times the comparison level in other coastal Alaska wolves and 278 times that in Interior Alaska wolves; the authors also reported that Pleasant Island wolf hair contained nearly eight times as much mercury as had been reported in Arctic wolf hair.

So while adapting to the otters has offered wolves a lifeline, it also raises unexpected problems the wolves now have to deal with.

“The ability of wolves to switch their diets from terrestrial prey to marine prey, just shows how resilient they can be. But we now know that their reliance on marine prey can also lead to the risk of toxicity,” Roffler said.

“We can assume that as sea otters continue to recolonize parts of their former range and grow in numbers, that wolves and other terrestrial predators will start using them as prey.”

The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

A separate peer-reviewed study published later in 2025 added another piece to the contaminant story. Researchers compared stable isotopes and trace elements in wolf hair from Pleasant Island, Gustavus, Juneau and Douglas Island. Populations making greater use of marine food showed distinctive isotope signatures and elevated concentrations of several trace elements. The result reinforces the link between marine foraging and contaminant exposure, although it likewise does not establish a population-level health effect.

Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

It was still dark off the Oregon coast on the morning of September 9, 1942, when the Japanese submarine I-25 rose to the surface. The Pacific was gray and restless. On deck the crew worked quickly, assembling a small floatplane—the Yokosuka E14Y, a fragile-looking craft of wood and fabric—and fitting it with two incendiary bombs. Warrant Officer Nobuo Fujita and his observer, Shoji Okuda, climbed aboard. The commander told Fujita he was going to make history. Then the little plane was catapulted into the sky and turned toward the dark line of the American shore.

Their purpose was as simple as it was ambitious. If they could set the forests of the Northwest ablaze, they might force the United States to look homeward, to pull men and machines away from the real fighting in the Pacific. They would show that even the mainland was not beyond reach.

Fujita flew inland over the Siskiyou National Forest near Brookings, over timber still wet from the rain of the night before. At the lookout tower on Mount Emily, a Forest Service man named Howard Gardner heard an engine that did not sound like the usual coastal patrols. He raised his glasses and saw the plane coming not along the shore but straight in, the red circles plain on its wings. A short time later two bombs fell on Wheeler Ridge. One started a fire. The other vanished into the woods.

That was the first time an enemy aircraft had dropped bombs on the contiguous United States in the Second World War.

What followed was not the inferno Tokyo had imagined. The ground was damp. Gardner and the other lookouts reached the smoke, kept it small, and held it until help arrived. The I-25 recovered its plane and slipped back under the sea. The newspapers in Japan proclaimed a great shock delivered to America. The shock was real enough. The damage was slight.

History often turns on such quiet collisions: a carefully laid plan meeting weather, and a few men who happened to be watching. Fujita had flown farther than any Axis pilot before him to strike the American mainland. The forest, and the people who knew it, simply would not burn the way the plan required. Years afterward he came back to Brookings, this time with an old family sword offered in friendship. The first air attack on the mainland ended not in flames, but in a reminder of how much depends on the ordinary vigilance of ordinary people, and on the land itself.

Jesuit Alumni in Congress
For the fifth consecutive session, Jesuit college alumni comprise ten percent of Congress. Of the 535 seats (and six non-voting delegate positions) in the 119th United States Congress, 55 are filled by graduates of Jesuit colleges and universities: 12 in the Senate and 43 in the House of Representatives.

Jesuit-educated members are well-represented in leadership positions in both the Senate and the House. In the Senate, Senator John Barrasso (R-WY, Georgetown) serves as Majority Whip; Senator Richard Durbin (D-IL, Georgetown) serves as Democratic Whip; and Senator Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV, Gonzaga) serves as Vice Chair of the Senate Democratic Outreach Committee. In the House, Representative Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY, Georgetown) serves as Democratic Leader; Representative Ted Lieu (D-CA, Georgetown) serves as Vice Chair of the House Democratic Caucus; Representative Debbie Dingell (D-MI, Georgetown) serves as Chair of the Democratic Policy and Communications Committee (DPCC); and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA, Georgetown) serves as Co-Chair of the DPCC.

Fifteen of the nation’s Jesuit colleges and universities have alumni who serve in the 119th U.S. Congress. Georgetown University has the most with a total of 25, followed by Boston College and Fordham University, each with six alumni (note: Representative Rosa DeLauro is an alumna of Marymount College, which was later incorporated by Fordham University). The College of the Holy Cross, Loyola Marymount University, Marquette University, Saint Louis University, Santa Clara University, University of Detroit Mercy and University of San Francisco all have two alumni represented. Creighton University, Gonzaga University, Loyola University Chicago, Regis University and The University of Scranton each have one alum.

In addition to the 55 alumni of Jesuit colleges and universities, graduates of Jesuit high schools are also serving in the 119th U.S. Congress.

text: Homeowners insurance rates have risen sharply in states like Florida and California for years. Now, the affordability crisis is spreading across the country. Nationwide, home insurance rates rose nearly 47% from 2020 through 2025, according to LendingTree's 2026 State of Home Insurance report. In the hardest-hit states, the 2025 jump was about three times the national average. Colorado saw rates jump 18.3%, while Minnesota and Iowa were close behind at 17% and 14.7%, respectively. No state included in LendingTree's analysis saw rates fall that year. Nebraska, which had the fifth-largest rate increase at 72%, now has the second-highest average homeowners insurance cost in the country at $4,956 a year. That's more than double the national average. Hail, wind, and wildfires have become the primary risk drivers. Bringing down insurance costs can involve: Shop around regularly,  Raise your deductible if you can afford it, Bundle home and auto coverage: Many insurers offer a multipolicy discount. Compare the combined price with the cost of buying the policies separately.  Ask about available discounts: Security systems, smoke detectors, and other safety features may qualify you for a discount. Some insurers also reward newer roofs or updated plumbing. Make your home more disaster resistant. Review your coverage limits and improve your credit score. (USA TODAY)

text:
9/11: A Detailed Overview
Chapter 3 — The 28 Pages (2/2)
Project 911DETAIL
Target anniversary: September 11, 2026

Part 2 of the 28-page file is the Riggs Bank money trail, the 1999 cockpit-door dry run, the Capitol videotape Scotland Yard seized in Birmingham, the firing of the investigator who wrote the pages, and why the 9/11 Commission's "no institutional funding" sentence is narrower than it sounds.

Part 1 closed with Fahad al-Thumairy's denials and his 2003 expulsion. Part 2 follows the money to Princess Haifa's Riggs Bank checks, then to the pre-9/11 dry run, the Capitol video the San Diego FBI never received, the Commission that followed, the internal document that shows its own investigators tried to keep pursuing these leads, and the second network — Sarasota — that Congress never saw at all.

Osama Bassnan and the Riggs Bank money trail

Osama Bassnan was a close associate of Bayoumi's who lived across the street from the hijackers in San Diego. He had previously listed employment with the Saudi Arabian Education Mission in Washington, a component of the Saudi embassy apparatus. After the attacks, he told an FBI asset that he "did more for the hijackers than Bayoumi did." The Joint Inquiry's files describe him as an outspoken supporter of Osama bin Laden, with reported connections to the Eritrean Islamic Jihad and to Omar Abdel-Rahman, the "Blind Sheikh" convicted in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing conspiracy. The FBI later said some of the early asset reporting on Bassnan could not be corroborated. Both the asset statement and the Bureau's caveat belong in the same paragraph.

The financial trail is the most specific element of Part Four, drawn from the Inquiry's citations to FBI files:

Beginning in January 1999, Princess Haifa bint Faisal — wife of Prince Bandar bin Sultan, then Saudi ambassador to the United States — maintained a standing order at Riggs Bank in Washington to send $2,000 a month to Bassnan's wife, described as support for thyroid medical treatment. The Inquiry noted it found "no evidence that Bassnan's wife provided nursing services" corresponding to that description.

A search of the Bassnan residence turned up 31 cashier's checks totaling $74,000, drawn on Princess Haifa's Riggs account, dated between February 22, 1999 and May 30, 2002.

On May 14, 1998, Bassnan personally cashed a $15,000 check drawn on Prince Bandar's own account. His wife separately cashed a $10,000 check from Princess Haifa's account on January 8, 1998.

Bayoumi's wife, Manal Bajadr (also rendered Bagader), attempted to deposit three of the checks made out to Bassnan's wife into her own account — an attempted diversion the Inquiry flagged as the documentary link between the ambassadorial household's money and the man who signed the hijackers' lease.

The Saudi explanation, offered publicly in 2002 when the story leaked, was routine zakat and medical charity: Bassnan had written the embassy in 1998 describing a wife who needed thyroid surgery. Secondary reporting noted that the wife's actual thyroid treatment did not occur until April 2000, two years after the initial appeal and after Hazmi and Mihdhar had already arrived in San Diego. That timing gap undercuts, without disproving, the charity explanation. The Commission's staff work on terrorist financing later stated there was no evidence this money was redirected to the hijackers. The Commission's final report separately stated: "We have found no evidence that Saudi Princess Haifa al Faisal provided any funds to the conspiracy, either directly or indirectly." Both things can be true at once: the money is documented; a completed pass-through to the hijackers is not.

The fallout reached beyond the individuals. Federal regulators assessed a $25 million civil penalty against Riggs Bank in 2004 for systemic Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money-laundering failures, tied in significant part to its handling of Saudi Embassy and related accounts — then the largest such civil penalty against a U.S. bank. The scandal, which also involved Equatorial Guinea accounts, effectively destroyed the institution. PNC Financial Services acquired Riggs in 2005. The penalty is not proof that embassy charity checks financed 9/11. It is proof that the bank of record for those checks was, by the regulator's finding, not monitoring large diplomatic flows the way the law required.

The pre-9/11 dry runs

In November 1999, two Saudi nationals with government ties — Mohammed al-Qudhaeein (spellings vary: al-Qudhaieen, al-Qudhai'een), employed in a student/Ministry of Islamic Affairs orbit, and Hamdan al-Shalawi — boarded an America West flight from Phoenix toward Washington. During the flight they asked attendants technical questions about the aircraft. Qudhaeein twice attempted to go forward toward the cockpit after being directed to a rear lavatory. The crew forced an emergency landing in Columbus, Ohio. The men were detained and questioned. Their tickets, they said, had been paid by the Saudi Embassy; they were traveling to an embassy event. The FBI did not prosecute. The men later sued America West for discrimination. CAIR publicly framed the episode as profiling.

After 9/11 the file looked different. The Joint Inquiry recorded the incident. The FBI's Phoenix Field Office treated it as a possible test of security procedures. Phoenix agent Kenneth Williams later stated in a sworn declaration that the office concluded the two men were conducting a possible dry run for a future hijacking; that the Saudi Embassy protested; and that the investigation was shut down shortly thereafter. Williams also stated that Shalawi and Qudhaeein had been in contact with future hijacker Hani Hanjour at a Tempe mosque, and that a car used by another Phoenix subject, Zacaria Soubra, was owned by Qudhaeein. Intelligence later indicated Qudhaeein had received explosives and car-bomb training in Afghanistan; his name went on a no-fly list. Shalawi was separately reported to have trained at camps in Afghanistan. A 2000 visa application by Qudhaeein to reenter the United States was denied.

This incident sits alongside, but is not identical to, the Phoenix Memo — Williams's July 10, 2001 warning about Islamist students at Arizona flight schools. They are adjacent threads. They should not be merged when Chapter 4 takes up Phoenix in depth. The 28 Pages put the cockpit-door episode in the Saudi-assistance file because of who paid the tickets and who the passengers turned out to be. That is the documented reason it is in this chapter.

The Capitol surveillance video

Ten days after the attacks, London's Metropolitan Police raided Bayoumi's Birmingham apartment, where he had relocated to study at Aston University. They seized roughly eighty videotapes and a trove of documents, including a tape recorded during a Washington trip in the summer of 1999. The footage shows Bayoumi filming the U.S. Capitol — entrances, security posts, a scale model of the building — while narrating in Arabic that he would "get over there" and "report to you in detail what is there," referencing "a plan" and noting the airport's proximity. A notepad seized in the same raid contained an aviation equation for calculating a plane's height and line-of-sight distance to the horizon, alongside a hand-drawn sketch of an aircraft.

British detectives, having interviewed Bayoumi over multiple days, believed the evidence met the threshold to request extradition. In a documented meeting, U.S. Department of Justice officials declined — after what participants describe as a conference call of about an hour — citing insufficient evidence. Bayoumi was released on September 28, 2001. Retired Detective Constable David Campbell, who conducted the interviews, later told The Sunday Times that the more he spoke with Bayoumi, the more he thought the man "needs to go before a court to answer it." In 2026 interviews with ITV he went further: he said two pieces of "game-changing" evidence — the Capitol video and the notebook — were not put in front of him during the interrogations, even though FBI officers were in the evidence chain and the material had been couriered toward the custody suite. That claim is Campbell's. It is consistent with later FBI chain-of-custody reconstructions. It is not a signed DOJ admission of concealment.

The handling of the video afterward is independently documented and damaging on its own, separate from the extradition decision. An internal FBI report dated October 11, 2001 states that copies of the seized exhibits were sent to FBI New York via Federal Express. The Capitol video never reached the San Diego field office that was actively investigating Bayoumi and the Parkwood complex. It was not before the 9/11 Commission when the Commission wrote its 2004 assessment of Bayoumi as an "unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists." Retired FBI agent Daniel Gonzalez, who worked the San Diego counterterrorism desk, has said he did not learn the video existed until 2024, when it surfaced in the civil litigation: "That angers me… When I saw that video, I knew exactly what it was." The notepad had a separate chain-of-custody gap: it sat uncatalogued in a Washington warehouse until an evidence technician's chance 2012 phone call to Gonzalez asking whether he wanted the boxes before they were destroyed.

Two readings of the tape now sit in the public record and should both be stated. Plaintiffs' experts and several former agents call it pre-operational surveillance of a target later assigned to United 93. Saudi Arabia and Bayoumi call it a tourist video. In an August 2025 ruling in the families' litigation, the New York court held that "all the Court can conclude" from the video is that Bayoumi "visited Washington DC and that he filmed the city." That judicial sentence does not erase the narration about a "plan," the security close-ups, or the notepad. It does mean a federal judge, looking at the same tape, refused to treat it as self-proving operational reconnaissance. Honest drafting holds both the agents' reading and the court's limit.

All original evidence seized in Birmingham — including the Capitol video and the notepad — was returned to Bayoumi. He remained free, completed a master's degree at Aston University, and returned to Saudi Arabia. He has never been charged.

"Document 17" and the dismissal of Dana Lesemann

Dana Lesemann and Michael Jacobson — the same two investigators who compiled the Saudi material for Part Four — moved to the 9/11 Commission staff and, on June 6, 2003, wrote a 47-page internal work plan addressed to Executive Director Philip Zelikow, Deputy Executive Director Chris Kojm, and General Counsel Dan Marcus. The document, now known as Document 17, proposed an extended list of questions regarding Saudi government links to the hijackers and asked whether "political, economic and other considerations" were shaping the U.S. government's willingness to investigate. Zelikow directed the pair to narrow an initial list of roughly twenty proposed lines of inquiry down to ten.

Lesemann was subsequently terminated. The immediate trigger, as reconstructed by Philip Shenon in The Commission and by later document releases, was her impatience with Zelikow's delay in granting her access to the classified 28 Pages — material she and Jacobson had themselves authored for the Joint Inquiry. She obtained the document through a channel other than Zelikow. When he learned she had it, he fired her for mishandling classified information. The questions raised in Document 17 do not have corresponding answers in the Commission's public final report. The Interagency Security Classification Appeals Panel declassified the underlying document in July 2015. https://t.co/N5xbAS54qd and the Florida Bulldog published the first sustained public readings.

This belongs in the chapter. The characterization has to stay precise. The sourcing establishes that Document 17 exists, that its questions went unanswered in the public report, that Zelikow cut the interview list, and that Lesemann's termination followed an access dispute over the very pages she had written. It does not, on the sourcing reviewed here, establish Zelikow's motive with certainty. Neutral accounts treat it as a personnel and classification fight. Pointed accounts — including Shenon's reporting on Zelikow's prior relationship with Condoleezza Rice and his role on the Bush transition — frame it as a structural conflict of interest that narrowed the Saudi inquiry. The second characterization should be attributed to its sources, not stated as a proven institutional decision to suppress.

The Sarasota network

Separately from the California network, FBI agents investigated a Saudi family — Abdulaziz al-Hijji, his wife Anoud, and her father Esam Ghazzawi, an adviser to a Saudi prince — who lived in the gated Prestancia community in Sarasota, Florida. About two weeks before the attacks (Florida Department of Law Enforcement records cited in later reporting give a departure around August 27, 2001), the family left the country, abandoning cars, food, and personal effects. Security-gate logs and later source accounts alleged that vehicles associated with hijackers Mohamed Atta, Ziad Jarrah, and Marwan al-Shehhi — training at nearby Venice flight schools — had visited the residence. An April 2002 FBI field communication stated that the family had "many connections" to "individuals associated with the terrorist attacks on 9/11/2001."

The FBI did not disclose this investigation to the Joint Inquiry or the 9/11 Commission at the time. Graham has said he did not learn of it until 2011, through journalists. Kean, Hamilton, and Zelikow later told him they had not been told either. FOIA litigation by the Florida Bulldog forced release of a large cache of related FBI documents. A 2015 FBI-sponsored review — the "9/11 Review Commission," chaired by Edwin Meese, with Tim Roemer and Bruce Hoffman — dismissed the connection as based on a "poorly written" and unsubstantiated 2002 field memo. The Bureau told that panel the agent who wrote the memo could not later explain its basis. The same review process produced a memorandum stating the FBI "did not obtain the gate records from the community because there was not a justified reason to believe there was a connection with the hijackers." Graham called that statement stunning. The Review Commission had no public hearings and no subpoena power of its own in the sense the original Commission did. This chapter treats its Sarasota conclusion as contested, not settled, because of that structural closeness to the agency whose files it was reviewing.

Sarasota is not in the 28 Pages. It is in this chapter because it is the other major alleged support node the Inquiry never saw, and because Graham has treated the two files as parts of the same unfinished question.

Part Four against the Commission's verdict

The 9/11 Commission's July 2004 report stated: "Saudi Arabia has long been considered the primary source of al Qaeda funding, but we have found no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution or senior Saudi officials individually funded the organization." It also stated it had seen no evidence that any foreign government or foreign government official supplied funding to the hijackers themselves. Those sentences are narrower than they are often read to be. They do not address mid-level diplomats, state-funded clerics, or individuals the Commission itself could not clear of intelligence-service ties. The parenthetical that immediately follows the institutional-funding sentence in the report — that the conclusion "does not exclude the likelihood that charities with significant Saudi government sponsorship diverted funds to al Qaeda" — is routinely dropped when the sentence is quoted as a full exoneration. It should not be dropped here.

Several Commissioners later said the report was never meant to be read as a full exoneration. Bob Kerrey stated that "significant questions remain unanswered concerning possible involvement of Saudi government institutions and actors," and that the report "should never have been read as an exoneration of Saudi Arabia." John Lehman said the same in substance and, in 2016, told interviewers that as many as several Saudi officials appeared in the assistance file, while still affirming the finding against the government "as an institution" and against senior officials as funders of al-Qaeda. Kean and Hamilton, by contrast, continued to emphasize that the Commission's own investigation had implicated only a tightly limited set of official names — with Thumairy the one most often cited — and had not found institutional direction of the plot. The split among Commissioners is itself evidence. The report's sentence was a negotiated product. Later affidavits in the families' litigation show how contested that product became.

The Commission's published account of Bayoumi called him "an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists." That characterization predates the Canestraro declaration's payroll figures, the documented DOJ extradition decline, the Capitol video's late arrival in San Diego, the 2017 GIP-cooptee memo, and Operation Encore's restaurant-meeting reconstruction — material the Commission did not have, did not pursue to the end, or, if Document 17 is read as its authors intended, was structurally discouraged from pursuing. Philip Shenon's reconstruction is that Zelikow and Dieter Snell rewrote the most damning Saudi passages before the report went to the printer. Zelikow has denied steering the investigation to protect the Kingdom or the White House. Both the rewrite claim and the denial are part of the historiography. Neither substitutes for the documents.

What can be said without overclaiming

A disciplined chapter can hold the following at once: fifteen of the nineteen hijackers were Saudi nationals — demography, not institutional proof. The first two hijackers to enter the United States received concrete help in Southern California from men who were paid by, credentialed by, or in repeated contact with Saudi government organs — Bayoumi through the PCA/Dallah Avco channel, Thumairy through the Ministry of Islamic Affairs and the Los Angeles consulate, Bassnan through ambassadorial household checks. The Joint Inquiry put those facts in writing in 2002 and said it had not verified their meaning. The Commission, with more time, issued a narrow institutional clearance and a soft personal clearance of Bayoumi that later files have eroded without producing a criminal case. No released U.S. government finding states that the King, the Crown Prince, or the cabinet directed the attacks — claiming that is an overreach the 28 Pages themselves refuse. And no released U.S. government finding fully explains why two linguistically unprepared al-Qaeda operatives were met, housed, banked, and socially embedded within days of arrival by a man whose government stipend multiplied in the same window — leaving that unexplained is also an overreach.

The 28 Pages are the inventory. They are not the trial.

Handoff to Chapter 4

Part Four ends where it began: a compilation, referred back to the FBI and CIA for further investigation, with the Joint Inquiry stating explicitly it had not verified what it found. This chapter has shown where that referral led when it reached agencies and litigants with the time and mandate the Inquiry lacked — some leads corroborated (the Ercan/Dallah allowance timing, already in the declassified Inquiry text; the Birmingham seizure and the DOJ extradition decline; Document 17's existence and Lesemann's firing; the Riggs penalty), some still requiring reconciliation (the exact King Fahad Mosque funding figure; competing Thumairy–Bayoumi call counts; whether Bassnan's checks ever reached hijacker accounts; what the Prestancia gate logs actually contain), and some, per the Commission's later critics, never pursued in public.

Chapter 4 picks up the FBI's own secret continuation of this file — Operation Encore — including the eventual identification of Musaed al-Jarrah as the alleged command node above Bayoumi and Thumairy, the GIP cooptee finding that recasts Bayoumi's "student" cover, and the question the 28 Pages asked and did not answer: whether the help in San Diego was hospitality, freelancing, or tasking.

AN OFFER TO OUR FRIENDS IN TALLAHASSEE

First, thank you to the Florida State fans who greeted us this weekend. Genuinely warm people. Several pulled me aside and quietly admitted they were pulling for SMU.

I told them we understood their pain and that we were only in town to help them find a new coach.

That was extremely well received.

Now, having spent a weekend in Tallahassee, I have a theory.

All that noise when SMU joined the ACC, all the bluster from that administration about what we were and what we had done and whether we belonged, was cover.

Florida State is a broken athletic department. Not a proud one having a rough patch. Broken. A poverty program with excellent uniforms.

The lights went out. On Monday night. On ESPN. In front of the country.

And here is the thing about SMU. We know what it is to have been great and then not be. We spent decades in that wilderness and we did it without a conference willing to have us and without a television deal, and we bought our way back into this league by taking zero media revenue for nine years.

So we do not mock the fallen. We help.

Here is our formal offer.

SMU will cover the electric bills for Florida State's athletic facilities. All of them. Indefinitely.

We will send our own electrical engineering faculty and a crew of licensed electricians to survey and repair your infrastructure. We are told the phrase in the industry is load capacity, and we would like you to have some.

We will fix the bathrooms. Nobody has asked us to. We are doing it anyway.

We will advise on how to spend money on athletes who actually perform, which is a discipline SMU has been refining since well before it was legal.

And we will help you find a coach. We will start in the Texas high school ranks, since we understand that is a proven pipeline for your program.

We ask for one thing in return.

Rename the stadium. Not much. Just the first name stays and the last name goes.

Doak Walker Stadium.

The house that Doak rebuilt.

Doak Walker won the Heisman at SMU in 1948 and was so popular they had to expand the Cotton Bowl twice to hold the crowds, which is why it has been called the House That Doak Built for seventy five years.

This would be his second stadium. He would have loved that. He was the kind of man who would have driven to Tallahassee himself with a toolbox.

Same first name. Better story. Working lights.

Think it over, Seminoles. The offer stands until you beat somebody.

Picked this up at the Greenville Equity Marketing Session earlier this month:

Instead of asking, "Would you take (description of offer)?"

Just state, "I'll take it with (description of offer)."

⬆️ I dig it. It avoids setting up "no" as one of the two responses the seller's mind thinks of before they've even heard the offer.

And subtley it forces their unconscious mind to envision a future in which they accept your offer. 

Kinda like when you were in middle school: 

"Will you go to the dance with me?"

vs

"I'll take you to the dance!"

Way more power in the second version.

Whiskey Jug Genie by Sultonna Nadine is a lighthearted and charming paranormal fantasy that mixes magic, humor, and a touch of romance for pure escapist fun.

When quiet London apothecary shop owner Martin buys an old whiskey jug on vacation, he has no idea he’s about to release Bubba, a genie who’s been trapped inside for 200 years and is thoroughly out of touch with the modern world. Chaos, spells, cultural clashes, and plenty of laughs ensue as the unlikely pair (along with a very annoyed cat) try to navigate the mess. Set against the backdrop of contemporary London with elements of white magic and everyday wonder, the story balances humorous situations with warmer moments. Readers appreciate its playful tone, quirky characters, and the perfect blend of paranormal fantasy, magic, and comedy—it’s the kind of book that delivers smiles and a welcome dose of whimsy.

Sultonna Nadine is the pen name used by Mellie Miller for her standalone fantasy romance novels that feature magic, alternate touches, and paranormal elements outside her main series. Born in the 1950s in the American Midwest, she has lived across the country, drawing on a rich background that includes music, martial arts, and Reiki. Married for decades to her husband Steve, she is a mother and grandmother who now lives in rural Georgia. Under this name she creates light, magical stories meant to offer readers an escape filled with romance and wonder. (She also writes series fiction as Mellie Miller.)

Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. text:
Landmark study reveals century-long U.S. suicide rate cycles among youth | University of Utah Health

Suicide rates in the United States follow striking, decades-long cycles likely shaped by broad social forces, according to a major study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). But beneath that long-term rise-and-fall pattern, researchers uncovered a deeply concerning and persistent trend: suicide risk among young people has been rising steadily for more than half a century, affecting each new generation earlier in life.

The findings demonstrate that suicide cannot be understood solely as a matter of individual psychology or biology, but that social context plays an important role, supporting a viewpoint that may spark a fresh approach to suicide prevention efforts.

This new study, co-led by Nina de Lacy of Huntsman Mental Health Institute at the University of Utah, draws on 122 years of U.S. mortality data spanning 1900 to 2021. By combining historically fragmented federal records into the new STACK (Suicide Trends and Archival Comparative Knowledgebase) dataset—the research team, which included faculty from the U College of Social and Behavioral Science, offers the most comprehensive long-term picture of U.S. suicide trends ever assembled.

“This is one of the first times we’ve been able to step back and see suicide clearly in a long-term historical context,” said de Lacy, an assistant professor of psychiatry. “What we found challenges the idea that today’s suicide crisis is purely recent or driven only by individual mental health factors. Suicide appears to be powerfully shaped by what’s happening in society—economically, socially and culturally—and those forces operate over decades.”

Suicide moves in cycles, unlike most other causes of death

The researchers found that overall U.S. suicide rates exhibit a rare cyclical pattern, rising and falling approximately every 10 to 25 years. Peaks occurred during periods of major social upheaval, including growing industrialization in the early 1910s, the Great Depression in the 1930s and the expansion of the women’s rights movement in the 1970s.

“Very few causes of death behave like this,” de Lacy said. “Heart disease, cancer and motor vehicle deaths generally decline when effective interventions are introduced. Suicide doesn’t follow that pattern. It fluctuates, reverses direction and resists long-term reduction.”

Despite these cycles and a recent uptick beginning in the early 2000s, the study shows that U.S. suicide rates are not currently at their highest historical levels, countering frequently made claims based on data covering shorter time frames. However, the researchers estimate that, if the nation had consistently maintained its lowest observed age-specific suicide rates, 372,365 deaths could have been prevented between 1969 and 2021.

A youth crisis that began decades earlier than we thought

The most troubling finding, the researchers note, is the long-term rise in suicide among young people. While public attention often focuses on recent increases among adolescents and young adults, the study found that this trend began in the mid-to-late 1950s—far earlier than previously recognized.

“What we’re seeing is not a short-term spike but a generational shift,” de Lacy said. “Each successive generation has faced higher suicide risk at a younger age than the one before it. That pattern has now persisted for more than 60 years.”

Historically, suicide risk was highest among older adults. Over time, that age divide has narrowed as rates declined among older Americans but climbed among those under 35, including children and adolescents. Today, suicide is among the leading causes of death for people ages 10 to 34.

Surprising shifts in geography and method

The analysis also revealed several unexpected changes in suicide risk patterns:

- Living in large metropolitan areas has emerged as a protective factor, with consistently lower suicide rates than in rural and smaller urban areas since the early 1980s.

- While suicide rates remain higher in rural areas overall, recent increases have been especially pronounced among women in rural and smaller urban communities.

- Suicide by hanging has risen sharply since the 1980s among both males and females, forming what the researchers describe as a “hidden epidemic” that has received less attention than firearm-related deaths, which continue to account for the majority of suicide deaths.

Rethinking suicide as a social phenomenon

The findings reinforce the idea that suicide cannot be understood solely as a matter of individual psychology or biology. Social context matters, often in ways that unfold slowly over generations.

“We can observe them, but we have been mystified by suicide trends over decades,” said co-author Bernice Pescosolido, director of the Irsay Institute for Sociomedical Research at Indiana University. “But this study and this new dataset are opening up new ideas that we really need to think about.”

De Lacy emphasized the implications for prevention efforts.

“If suicide risk rises and falls with broader social conditions, then prevention has to go beyond the clinic,” she said. “We need tailored strategies that address connectedness, community, economic stability and the lived experience of entire generations, not just interventions targeted at individuals after they’re already in crisis.”

If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available. The Suicide & Crisis Lifeline is available 24 hours a day by calling or texting 988.

The SEC accusing LSU of “lack of institutional control” hits differently when you look at the timeline:

2011-12 — NCAA major-infractions case. Recruiting violations. LSU put on probation.

2012-17 — Booster John Paul Funes provides $180K in impermissible benefits to a football player’s family using money embezzled from a hospital foundation.

2013 — Les Miles investigation intentionally stored offsite. AD Joe Alleva recommends firing him. LSU keeps him.

2017-19 — Will Wade caught on FBI wiretap discussing a “strong-ass offer.”

2019 — LSU suspends Wade after he refuses to meet with LSU/NCAA officials. Reinstates him 5 weeks later.

2020 — LSU’s handling of sexual misconduct allegations exposed.

2020 — Odell Beckham Jr. hands LSU players cash after the national title.

2020 — LSU self-imposes scholarship cuts, recruiting restrictions and a bowl ban amid the NCAA investigation.

LSU’s statement:

“This decision reflects LSU’s commitment to compliance with NCAA regulations and maintenance of institutional control.”

2021 — Independent review finds systemic Title IX failures. Verge Ausberry suspended 30 days without pay.

2022 — LSU fires Wade after an NCAA Notice of Allegations containing multiple Level I allegations.

2022 — Separate NCAA case: Football commits COVID dead-period recruiting violations. One year probation.

2023 — IARP resolves the football/basketball case: multiple violations, failure to monitor, 37 football wins vacated and 3 more years probation, beginning when the prior probation ended Sept. 21, 2023.

The NCAA also alleged lack of institutional control. The IARP did not sustain that allegation.

2024 — LSU pays $1.9M to settle Title IX claims. No admission of liability.

2026 — LSU rehires Will Wade.

The AD announcing the hire? Verge Ausberry.

2026 — Wade pursues international pros, an NBA draft pick and players with professional basketball experience.

2026 — LSU pursues outside capital tied to future SEC media revenue.

2026 — LSU pushes to add players who signed NFL contracts and went through NFL camps.

Sept. 2026 — The SEC sues LSU. Ausberry is a named defendant.

LSU ultimately leaves the former NFL players off its final roster.

The SEC presses forward anyway.

Its amended complaint says LSU’s actions “confirm the lack of institutional control over the athletics program at LSU that is required by Article 6 of the SEC Constitution.”

At the informal direction of the other 15 SEC presidents and chancellors, Sankey calls a Special Meeting for Sept. 10 to consider terminating LSU’s membership — whether LSU backs off the professional players or not.

And LSU is still on NCAA probation.

It expires Sept. 21.

Twelve days from now.

Different coaches. Different scandals.

Same institution. And in some cases, the same people.

Profile

Jerry Lawler

It’s good to be the king. Just ask Jerry Lawler.

Reigning over sports-entertainment since the 1970s, Jerry “The King” Lawler has thrilled in the ring as the fighting pride of Memphis, Tenn. and entertained from the announce table as Raw’s most irrepressible broadcaster. Effective as both a hero and villain, The King enraged WWE fans when he offended Bret Hart’s mother during a personal rivalry with The Hit Man and then inspired them when he stepped in the ring to challenge The Miz for the WWE Title at 61 years of age. This aptitude for every aspect of sports-entertainment has earned Lawler countless titles, legions of fans and entry into the WWE Hall of Fame.

Before all that, though, The King made his name in the Tennessee area prior to gaining national attention for his rivalry with comedian Andy Kaufman. Andrew Geoffrey "Andy" Kaufman (January 17, 1949 – May 16, 1984) was an American entertainer, actor and performance artist. The film was directed by Johnny Legend, who employed his sister Lynne Margulies as one of the women who appears in the film. Margulies met Kaufman for the first time on camera, and they later became a couple, living together until Kaufman's death.

In 2002 Kaufman became an unlockable character in the video game Legends of Wrestling II and a standard character in 2004's Showdown: Legends of Wrestling.

TV Guide listed Jerry "The King" Lawler slapping Andy Kaufman on Late Show with David Letterman in 1982 as "1 of 60 Most Riveting Moments in TV History."

This pseudo angle have nothing to do with Vince McMahon's then named World Wrestling Federation, but came out of the USWA territory. TV Guide lists Jerry "The King" Lawler slapping Andy Kaufman as historic television moment

(In Case You Missed It)

Wrestling News Media

20th August 2013

TV Guide listed Jerry "The King" Lawler slapping Andy Kaufman on Late Show with David Letterman in 1982 as "1 of 60 Most Riveting Moments in TV History."

From Hollywood to Memphis, Tennessee, to Sydney, Australia and beyond, you have probably heard of the classic Lawler - Kaufman feud. It was Hollywood VS Pro wrestling. This pseudo angle have nothing to do with Vince McMahon's then named World Wrestling Federation, but came out of the USWA territory. One ponders if Mr McMahon might try to recreate something extremely similar to this for today's sports entertainment audience. McMahon did the Mickey Rourke angle with Roddy Piper, Ricky Steamboat and Ric Flair, with WWE Superstar Chris Jericho in the mix, but that was far from a carbon copy of the classic Lawler VS Kaufman angle. You can watch the classic Letterman show segment here.

Jerry Lawler Slaps Andy Kaufman | Letterman
https://t.co/rIbotBvTIt

Things get ugly when Andy Kaufman and Jerry Lawler try to work out their differences with Dave. (Air date: 7/28/82)

#AndyKaufman #JerryLawler #Letterman

Profile

Jerry Lawler

It’s good to be the king. Just ask Jerry Lawler.

Reigning over sports-entertainment since the 1970s, Jerry “The King” Lawler has thrilled in the ring as the fighting pride of Memphis, Tenn. and entertained from the announce table as Raw’s most irrepressible broadcaster. Effective as both a hero and villain, The King enraged WWE fans when he offended Bret Hart’s mother during a personal rivalry with The Hit Man and then inspired them when he stepped in the ring to challenge The Miz for the WWE Title at 61 years of age. This aptitude for every aspect of sports-entertainment has earned Lawler countless titles, legions of fans and entry into the WWE Hall of Fame.

Before all that, though, The King made his name in the Tennessee area prior to gaining national attention for his rivalry with comedian Andy Kaufman. Claiming to be the "Inter-Gender Wrestling Champion of the World,” Kaufman made the mistake of insulting The King in front of his hometown crowd in the Mid-South Coliseum in 1982. Lawler responded by blasting the “Taxi” actor with two piledrivers, which led to an incendiary showdown on “Late Night with David Letterman.” During a tense interview on the program, Kaufman once again offended The King, leading Lawler to slap the comic right out of his chair in front of a shocked studio audience. Fifteen years later, the WWE Hall of Famer recreated this legendary TV moment with Jim Carrey on the set of the Andy Kaufman biopic, “Man on the Moon.”

After dispatching of Kaufman, The King ruled over promotions like Minnesota’s AWA and Tennessee’s USWA before finally arriving in WWE in 1992. Caustic from the get go, Lawler used his sharp wit to rile up rivals like Bret “Hit Man” Hart and Doink the Clown before taking a seat at the announce booth to commentate alongside Jim Ross. Together, the duo formed one of sports-entertainment’s most entertaining broadcast teams as they deftly called the action of WWE’s booming “Attitude Era.”

Lawler’s voice has remained a staple of WWE programming ever since, but that hasn’t stopped him from getting in the ring. Often noted as one of the greatest Superstars to never hold the WWE Championship, The King nearly beat The Miz for the coveted title at Elimination Chamber in 2011 and took on his snivelling broadcast partner, Michael Cole, at WrestleMania XXVII. Competing in his fifth decade as a wrestler, Lawler proved that his piledriver — just like his wit — was still as devastating as ever. (WWE)

Andy Kaufman...

Andrew Geoffrey "Andy" Kaufman (January 17, 1949 – May 16, 1984) was an American entertainer, actor and performance artist. While often referred to as a comedian, Kaufman did not consider himself to be one. He disdained telling jokes and engaging in comedy as it was traditionally understood, referring to himself instead as a "song-and-dance man." Elaborate ruses and pranks were major elements of his career. His body of work maintains a cult following and he continues to be respected for his original material, performance style, and unflinching commitment to character.

Professional wrestling

Kaufman grew up admiring the world of professional wrestling. Inspired by the theatricality of kayfabe, the staged nature of the sport, and his own tendency to form elaborate hoaxes, Kaufman began wrestling women during his act and was the self-proclaimed "Inter-Gender Wrestling Champion of the World", taking on an aggressive and ridiculous personality based upon the characters invented by professional wrestlers. He offered a $1,000 prize to any woman who could pin him. He employed performance artist Laurie Anderson, a friend of his, as a stooge in this act for a while.

Kaufman initially approached the head of the World Wrestling Federation, Vince McMahon Sr. about bringing his act to the New York wrestling territory. McMahon dismissed Kaufman's idea as the elder McMahon was not about to bring "show business" into his Pro Wrestling society.

Kaufman had by then developed a friendship with Wrestling magazine reporter/photographer Bill Apter. After many discussions about Andy wanting to be in the Pro Wrestling business, Apter called Memphis' iconic Jerry "The King" Lawler and introduced him to Kaufman by telephone from Apter's apartment in Queens, New York. The battles between Kaufman and Lawler became legend and was really the first "sports entertainment" angle that became known worldwide and is being seen even today on TV stations such as Comedy Central.

Later, after a challenge from professional wrestler Jerry "The King" Lawler, Kaufman would step into the ring (in the Memphis wrestling circuit) with a man—Lawler himself. Kaufman taunted the whole city of Memphis, sending "videos showing residents how to use soap" and proclaiming it to be "the nation's redneck capital." Their ongoing feud, often featuring Jimmy Hart and other heels in Kaufman's corner, included a broken neck for Kaufman as a result of Lawler's piledriver and a famous on-air fight on a 1982 episode of Late Night with David Letterman. For some time after that, Kaufman appeared wearing a neck brace, insisting that his injuries were worse than they were. Kaufman would continue to defend the Inter-Gender Championship in the Mid-South Coliseum and offered an extra prize, other than the $1,000: that if he were pinned, the woman who pinned him would get to marry him and that Kaufman would also shave his head.

Kaufman and Lawler's famous feud and wrestling matches were later revealed to have been staged, or a "work", as the two were actually friends. The truth about it being a "work" was not disclosed until more than 10 years after Kaufman's death, when the Emmy-nominated documentary, A Comedy Salute to Andy Kaufman, aired on NBC in 1995. Coincidentally, Jim Carrey, the one who revealed the secret, later went on to play Kaufman in the 1999 film Man on the Moon. In a 1997 interview with the Memphis Flyer, Lawler claimed he had improvised during their first match and the Letterman incident.

Although officials at St. Francis Hospital stated that Kaufman's neck injuries were real, in his 2002 biography It's Good to Be the King ... Sometimes, Lawler detailed how they came up with the angle and kept it quiet. Even though Kaufman's injury was legitimate, the pair pretended that the injury was more severe than it was. He also said that Kaufman's explosion on Letterman was Kaufman's own idea, including when Lawler slapped Kaufman out of his chair. Promoter Jerry Jarrett would later recall that for two years, he would mail pay checks to Kaufman, with payments comparable to what other main event wrestlers were getting at the time, but Kaufman never cashed any of them.

Kaufman also appeared in the 1983 film My Breakfast with Blassie with professional wrestling personality "Classy" Freddie Blassie, a parody of the art film My Dinner With Andre. The film was directed by Johnny Legend, who employed his sister Lynne Margulies as one of the women who appears in the film. Margulies met Kaufman for the first time on camera, and they later became a couple, living together until Kaufman's death.

In 2002 Kaufman became an unlockable character in the video game Legends of Wrestling II and a standard character in 2004's Showdown: Legends of Wrestling.

Jerry Lawler Discusses His Feud With Andy Kaufman On Its 30th Anniversary - 28th July 2012 (Credit: WWE)

To recognize the 30th anniversary of the famous incident on The David Letterman Show, Jerry Lawler discussed his legendary feud with Taxi star Andy Kaufman in an interview with the official WWE website. Lawler went in-depth on his relationship with Kaufman, how Kaufman got involved in the wrestling business, how unscripted the Letterman incident was, and more.

In the following excerpt, Lawler explains what has made the rivalry so legendary, as well as Kaufman’s impact on the industry, which leads to him saying that Kaufman should be in the WWE Hall of Fame:

WWE CLASSICS: Out of all the great rivalries in wrestling and all the great pop culture moments, what is it about this one incident that 30 years later people are still so fascinated by?

LAWLER: It was the first time something like that had happened. I don’t know if I should tell this or not, but one night I was flying back on the plane with Vince McMahon. And he said, “You know, King, I’ve never told you this before, but I was so jealous when you got Andy Kaufman and did all that stuff with him down there in Memphis. Because he was from New York, and I thought we could have done all that stuff up here.” But he also said, “But I’ll be honest with you. There’s no way on Earth we could have done it as well as you guys did it.”

WWE CLASSICS: Wow. It would have been a totally different dynamic.

LAWLER: Yes, but it would have been a first. Vince loves firsts. To this day, you hear on Monday Night Raw that you’re going to see something for the first time ever. That’s big. And this was the first time any big deal Hollywood star was involved to that extent in wrestling. Vince realized, everybody realized, because it got so much national exposure. Everything back then was still regionalized. Cable TV hadn’t hit yet. The country was divided up into wrestling territories because of TV coverage. Once Vince saw you could use a Hollywood star to get that nationwide exposure, here comes Cyndi Lauper with Captain Lou and Wendi Richter, and then Mr. T gets brought in. The ball got rolling, and it hasn’t stopped to this day. Just in the past year, Hugh Jackman was in there punching Dolph Ziggler.

WWE CLASSICS: Yeah, you really could argue that Andy Kaufman is responsible for all of that.

LAWLER: I really feel, in my heart of hearts, that he was responsible for that. I certainly believe that Andy Kaufman deserves a spot in the celebrity wing of the WWE Hall of Fame. Without a doubt, we would not be where we are today without his involvement. I really feel that way. Even at Raw 1,000, we had Charlie Sheen challenging Daniel Bryan to a match. It’s Andy Kaufman revisited as recently as last night...

WWE CLASSICS: How soon did you know it was going to become a huge deal in the media?

LAWLER: As soon as it aired, my phone started blowing up. The New York Times, all the New York papers, everybody was calling. It just went ballistic.

WWE CLASSICS: This has become an iconic, not just wrestling moment, but a pop culture moment. After this gained legendary status, did you ever hear what Dave’s reaction was?

LAWLER: I heard that he was furious because it was so different than what was planned with his producers. I don’t think he was ever happy with it, but I also heard that his production staff referred to it for years as “The Famous Show.” That episode got so much attention and so much coverage, that they had to realize that this was one of the things that made Dave’s show famous.

WWE CLASSICS: It really went viral before there was an Internet.

LAWLER: Exactly. It is consistently listed as one of the top moments in the history of television. Thirty years later, I’m still doing interviews about it. We were talking to media just the other day for Raw 1,000, and every single one of them asked me about Andy Kaufman.

WWE CLASSICS: Out of all the great rivalries in wrestling and all the great pop culture moments, what is it about this one incident that 30 years later people are still so fascinated by?

LAWLER: It was the first time something like that had happened. I don’t know if I should tell this or not, but one night I was flying back on the plane with Vince McMahon. And he said, “You know, King, I’ve never told you this before, but I was so jealous when you got Andy Kaufman and did all that stuff with him down there in Memphis. Because he was from New York, and I thought we could have done all that stuff up here.” But he also said, “But I’ll be honest with you. There’s no way on Earth we could have done it as well as you guys did it.”

And this was the first time any big deal Hollywood star was involved to that extent in wrestling. Vince realized, everybody realized, because it got so much national exposure. Everything back then was still regionalized. Cable TV hadn’t hit yet. The country was divided up into wrestling territories because of TV coverage. Once Vince saw you could use a Hollywood star to get that nationwide exposure, here comes Cyndi Lauper with Captain Lou and Wendi Richter, and then Mr. T gets brought in. The ball got rolling, and it hasn’t stopped to this day. Just in the past year, Hugh Jackman was in there punching Dolph Ziggler.

LAWLER: I really feel, in my heart of hearts, that he was responsible for that. I certainly believe that Andy Kaufman deserves a spot in the celebrity wing of the WWE Hall of Fame. Without a doubt, we would not be where we are today without his involvement. I really feel that way. Even at Raw 1,000, we had Charlie Sheen challenging Daniel Bryan to a match. It’s Andy Kaufman revisited as recently as last night.

WWE CLASSICS: Where does Andy rank in the pantheon of great villains in wrestling? He was right up there.

LAWLER: He really was. To be a great villain, you’ve gotta get personal. And that’s what Andy did. He got personal with the people of Memphis by insulting their hygiene, and it went beyond just being about wrestling. He made things personal by insulting the fans themselves rather than just me. If he had ever gotten to do that on a national level, he just would have gotten better and better. He was a natural at it. He even created that sleazy lounge singer character named Tony Clifton just so he could play the bad guy. He wanted that reaction. Andy was a heel at heart. (Credit: WWE)

text:
THE SCOUTING CLASSROOM
Stories Behind the Report

HE DIDN’T LOOK LIKE A PROSPECT. HE JUST KEPT HITTING.

The body made scouts hesitate. The barrel kept giving us the answer.

My first year scouting for the Angels in 2000, Salt Lake CC had a catcher/first baseman named Chris Shelton who could hit.

And I mean really hit.

The problem was Chris didn’t look like a prospect.

THE BODY

He didn’t have the sculpted, get-off-the-bus V-shaped body scouts dream about. He looked more like former Phillies slugger Greg Luzinski.

But the more I watched Chris, the less I cared what he looked like.

He didn’t give away at-bats. He rarely struck out. He consistently found the sweet spot and drove line drives with authority.

As a freshman he hit .362 with 13 HR. As a sophomore, after Salt Lake CC moved to wood bats, he hit .402 and was Region 18 Player of the Year.

I needed to get closer.

THREE BATS

I arranged a private workout at his alma mater, Cottonwood HS. It would be the only private workout Chris did before the 2000 Draft.

I didn’t need to see him run or throw.

I wanted to control one thing: the hitting environment.

Chris started hitting ropes everywhere. I asked him to drive balls the other way. Balls disappeared into backyards. Center field? Off the wall or over it. Then I asked him to turn on balls.

Thunder.

One after another left the park with height and carry.

Afterward I asked to see his bat.

There was a 4–5 inch section of the barrel absolutely caked with ball marks.

The proverbial bull’s-eye.

“How many bats did you go through this spring?”

Remember, these were ash bats, not today’s harder maple.

Three

More than 50 games.

That got my attention.

The statistics told me Chris could hit. The barrel told me why.

THE TEST

Chris went undrafted and headed to the University of Utah.

Against better competition, he answered again:

.374 — 22 2B — 19 HR — 66 RBI.

Mountain West Player of the Year. All-American recognition.

I had him in the 8th–12th round range and brought him to Anaheim for our pre-draft workout.

During the live portion, future 1st Rd’er Jeremy Bonderman threw Chris a 97-mph fastball.

Chris launched it high and deep into the rock structure in dead center field at Angel Stadium.

Our scouting director Donny Rowland walked over.

“How much can we get this guy for?”

The body hadn’t changed.

The audience had.

THE DRAFT

Starting around the 15th round, the Angels repeatedly had me call Chris with offers.

We couldn’t get together on the money.

He kept sliding

Around the 30th round, Pirates scout Ted Williams called me asking what was happening with “my boy Shelton.”

Soon afterward Pittsburgh selected him in the 33rd round.

Chris signed for $25,000

And then he did what Chris Shelton had always done.

He hit.

He batted .307 across 10 minor-league seasons, hit .404 to win an Arizona Fall League batting title and MVP, and hit .273 over five Major League seasons, with Detroit, Texas and Seattle. 

Think about that.

Thirty-third round.

THE LESSON

The body matters. Projection matters. Athleticism matters.

But sometimes we make evaluation harder than it needs to be.

“At some point, you have to stop scouting what the player looks like, and start believing what the player does.”

Chris’s baseball story didn’t end when his playing career did. He returned to Cottonwood, winning two state championships as an assistant and head coach, and today he’s an assistant coach at Salt Lake CC, the NJCAA DI 2025 national champions.

More than 25 years after I first evaluated whether Chris Shelton looked like a prospect, he’s still impacting the game.

And maybe baseball had the answer all along.

Chris Shelton didn’t look like somebody’s idea of a prospect.

He just kept hitting.

text:
𝗪𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗡𝗼. 𝟮 (of 2)
1995
Charcoal on heavyweight paper
42” x 38” (h × w)
Artist collection

One of my early drawings from my second semester as a graduate student at the University of North Texas in Denton, Texas. I had left the comfort and familiarity of Tyler, Texas, where I had earned my Bachelor of Fine Arts degree at the University of Texas at Tyler. At UNT, I was floundering, both visually and mentally. I had gone from feeling established, confident, and certain of myself as an artist to feeling scared, uncertain, and very much like a stranger in a new place. 𝗪𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗡𝗼. 𝟮 represents those early drawings, which were cathartic, conceptual, simplified, and deliberately crude. Rather than illustrating subjects from a distance, I made artwork directly from what was happening internally. These drawings functioned as visual diaries of my moods, thoughts, and emotional states.

𝗪𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗡𝗼. 𝟮 is a psychologically charged figurative drawing in which a woman holding a wine glass and cigarette is approached by an unseen figure just beyond the left edge of the composition. The off-camera figure extends a hand toward her, and she accepts it, her right hand resting in the other person's palm as their fingers fold around hers. This quiet exchange becomes an intimate gesture of invitation, suggesting the possibility of a relationship, companionship, sexual encounter, one-night stand, or some other private experience beyond the visible frame.

The unseen figure is important because the invitation remains deliberately unresolved. We never see who is offering the hand or where that person intends to take her. Instead, the viewer is left to imagine what exists beyond the composition. Her expression is detached and difficult to read, creating tension between her apparent emotional distance and her unmistakable acceptance of the offered hand.

Formally, the figure emerges from dense, enveloping charcoal passages. Her pale face, arms, and torso contrast with the heavily worked darkness surrounding her, while strong contour lines define the hands, wine glass, cigarette, and face. The drawing moves between precise linear description and rubbed, smudged areas that dissolve into abstraction.

The combination of wine, cigarette, the unseen companion, and the accepted hand creates an atmosphere of temptation, intimacy, escape, and psychological ambiguity. The edge of the paper becomes almost a threshold to something we cannot see, leaving the most important part of the encounter outside the frame.
